# Webhook vs. Bot Account Tradeoffs

Covers capabilities, limitations, and when each is appropriate. See
[citations.md](../citations.md) for full source details.

## Capability Comparison

| Capability | Webhook | Bot Account |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| Send messages | Yes [6] | Yes |
| Send embeds | Yes (up to 10) [6] | Yes |
| Send files | Yes [6] | Yes |
| Send components (buttons, selects) | Application-owned only [6] | Yes |
| Send polls | Yes [6] | Yes |
| Read messages | **No** [6] | Yes (with intent) [1] |
| Receive events | **No** [6] | Yes (via gateway) [1] |
| Respond to interactions | **No** | Yes [2] |
| Display presence/status | **No** | Yes [10] |
| React to messages | **No** | Yes |
| Edit own messages | Yes (with message ID) | Yes |
| Delete own messages | Yes (with message ID) | Yes |
| Custom username per message | Yes [12] | No (fixed bot name) |
| Thread support | Yes (thread_id, thread_name) [6] | Yes |

Webhooks "operate one direction only — cannot read messages or receive
events. Designed for posting content, not monitoring or responding." [6]

## Why a Bot Account Is Needed

Any use case requiring **bidirectional communication** requires a bot account
connected via the gateway WebSocket: [1] [6]

- Reading message content (MESSAGE_CREATE events) [1]
- Responding to user interactions (slash commands, buttons) [2]
- Monitoring channel activity [1]
- Displaying online/offline presence [10]
- Reacting to messages [1]

A personal automation bot inherently needs to receive and respond, making a bot
account the required choice for the primary integration.

## Rate Limits

| Type | Limit | Source |
|------|-------|--------|
| Webhook execute | 5 requests per 2 seconds per webhook | [11] |
| Bot REST API (global) | 50 requests per second | [4] |
| Bot gateway events | 120 events per 60 seconds | [1] |
| Interaction responses | Exempt from global cap | [4] |

Webhook rate limits are per-webhook, so multiple webhooks can increase
aggregate throughput. However, "sporadic 429 errors even when headers suggest
capacity remains" are reported. [11]

## Security Comparison

| Aspect | Bot Token | Webhook URL |
|--------|-----------|-------------|
| Blast radius if leaked | All servers the bot is in | Single channel only |
| Access type | Read + write + modify | Write only |
| Authentication | Token in Authorization header | Embedded in URL |
| Rotation | Regenerate in Developer Portal | Delete and recreate webhook |
| Detection | GitGuardian detects separately | GitGuardian detects separately |

[26] [11]

A leaked bot token allows an attacker to "authenticate and interact with the
Discord API" as the bot, including sending messages, modifying servers, and
accessing data across **all servers** the bot occupies. [26]

A leaked webhook URL allows posting messages to **one channel** only. No HMAC
signatures or request-level authentication — "anyone who obtains the URL can
post messages to your channel." [11]

**For personal automation**: The bot token's blast radius is limited to a
single private server, reducing the risk substantially. Standard precautions
(`.env` file, never commit to VCS, rotate periodically) are sufficient. [26]

## When Webhooks Are Still Useful

Even with a bot account, webhooks serve specific purposes:

1. **External notifications**: CI/CD, monitoring alerts, cron jobs — a single
   POST is simpler than maintaining a WebSocket connection [6] [11]
2. **Isolation**: Services that only need to post can use a webhook URL instead
   of the bot token, limiting blast radius [26]
3. **Custom identity**: Webhooks can set a different username and avatar per
   message [12]

## Gaps and Limitations

- Webhook rate limit ("5 requests per 2 seconds") comes from the Hookdeck
  guide [11], not official Discord docs — official docs do not publish
  webhook-specific rate limits in the fetched sources
- Whether application-owned webhooks can send all component types or only a
  subset was not confirmed
- No data on webhook message editing rate limits
